clips.title: Claude Code Plugins: Share Your Setup With Your Team
clips.why: Why a team needs plugins at all: copied skills and settings drift apart, and new people never get them.
look: The problem with copy-pasting skills between people: every copy changes on its own.
Why one shared source matters more for a team than for one person.
clips.after: Managed settings take the next step: instead of asking people to install the shared plugin, the policy installs it for them.

clips.title: Claude Code Hooks, Explained Simply.
clips.why: A clear picture of what a hook is, when it runs in the agent's life, and why it gives you rules that hold whatever the model decides.
look: What a hook actually is: your program, started by Claude Code at a fixed moment.
The lifecycle events, and which one runs before a tool call.
The idea of adding determinism (the same answer every time) to an agent that is not deterministic.
clips.after: rhino-core's guard is a PreToolUse hook: it runs before every Write and Edit, and a model cannot argue with its exit code.

clips.title: Claude Code - Getting Started with Hooks
clips.why: You watch someone write a Python hook handler that reads the event from stdin, which is exactly how our guard works.
look: The handler reads the event as JSON from stdin and uses the fields it needs.
How the logic decides what to do for each kind of event.
clips.after: Our guard is the same shape, with one difference that matters: it answers with exit code 2 to block a write.

clips.title: 5.2 Claude Code CLAUDE.md & Settings: Scopes, Permissions & Precedence
clips.why: A short walk up the ladder of settings layers and the order in which they win.
look: Which settings file belongs to which scope, from personal to organization.
Which layer wins when two of them set the same key.
clips.after: Our policy uses the top of that ladder: what managed settings set, no laptop can undo.

practice.q: Your guard printed a reason on stderr and exited with code 2 on a Write. What happens next?

options.text: The Write is blocked and Claude reads the stderr text as the reason
options.why: Exit 2 is the blocking answer for PreToolUse, and stderr is how the hook explains itself.

options.text: The Write goes ahead and the message is only logged
options.why: That is what exit 0 does with stdout. Exit 2 blocks.
A hook decides one tool call. The session continues, and Claude can try another way.

practice.q: Finish the managed-settings line that forces rhino-core from the rhino marketplace on for everyone.
practice.why: enabledPlugins keys are plugin-name@marketplace-name. In managed settings, true forces the plugin on and false blocks it everywhere.

practice.q: Put the settings layers in order, from the one that wins to the one that loses.
practice.why: Managed settings are on top, your personal file is at the bottom, and the project files sit between them with your local file above the shared one.

practice.q: Two drop-ins both set allowedMcpServers: 40-mcp.json lists the dev3 server and 45-connectors.json lists the Atlassian server. Which servers are allowed?

options.text: Only Atlassian, because the later file wins
options.why: The later file wins only for single values. Lists are combined.

options.text: Both, because lists from drop-ins are combined
options.why: Drop-ins merge in name order: single values are replaced, lists are combined, objects merge key by key.

options.text: Neither, because the two files conflict
options.why: There is no conflict for lists; they simply add up.

practice.q: On a Mac, which folder holds the drop-in files of a file-based policy?
practice.hint: The file name of the main policy, with .d instead of .json.
practice.why: managed-settings.json and the managed-settings.d/ folder sit side by side in the system folder; the drop-ins merge after the main file, in alphabetical order.
